newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thai refiners cushioned from price slump.
newsitem.headline: Thai refiners cushioned from price slump.

text.p: A vibrant domestic market is cushioning Thai refiners from needing to cut output in the wake of collapsing oil product prices, but they may be forced to do so within a month, industry sources said on Tuesday.

"Our product prices are higher (than Singapore)...so our margins are better, but margins are getting smaller. If the situation continues we may be forced to cut production," one Thai refining source said.
"The Thai market is less sensitive to international demand because of the large domestic market," another refiner said.
In the past two weeks, gas oil prices in Singapore have slumped more than $6.00 per barrel, or about 20 percent, while fuel oil has lost around $28 per tonne, or 22 percent.
They were assessed on Tuesday at $25.75 per barrel and $96.00 per tonne respectively.
The slump prompted Shell Singapore to cut runs more than five percent, Esso to cut 20/25 percent and Singapore Refining Co said it would cut 10/15,000 bpd, or about five percent.
Thai refiners might cut runs as early as February as "nobody wants to lose money", but because they have commitments of crude purchases immediate cuts were not possible, the refinery source said.
Some Thai refiners said they would consider bringing forward plant maintenance, if weak prices persisted, in an effort to limit production losses because of the weak margins.
"The low margin situation is coming so early. We need to check with the other services to see if the turnaround can be brought forward," the refining source said.
Refining profits are usually at their lowest during the second quarter, following the peak demand winter season. Refiners usually schedule plant maintenance for this time.
Thai refining margins were estimated at $2.00 per barrel above Singapore, where profits slumped into the red last Friday with some refiners losing up to $1.50 per barrel processed.
A Thai Oil source estimated its average refinery margin for 1995/96 (Oct-Sept) at $4.48 per barrel, compared to $2.50 in Singapore.

Bigger profits were helped by strong demand. Domestic consumption of refined products rose 9.5 percent to 772,000-bpd year-on-year in the first 11 months of 1996, the Petroleum Authority of Thailand (PTT) said this month.
Thai refining sources said demand would have grown further since, because December marked the start of a period of high demand in the wake of the monsoon season.
They said post-monsoon demand was expected to grow by 5-10 percent compared with demand during the monsoon season.
But not all of the Thai demand is supplied by local refiners. Imports of refined products Jan-Nov 1996 averaged 147,000-bpd, PTT data showed.
Imports of gasoline, gas oil, aviation fuel (jet fuel) and fuel oil fell between 12.7 and 65.4 percent year-on-year, but not enough to prompt Thai refiners to operate at maximum rate.
They currently operate about 10 percent below maximum rate. The sector raised output capacity in 1996 by 275,000-bpd to 760,000-bpd. About five percent of output is exported.
"The newer refineries are operating at lower rates because they have to export some of their product," one source said.
Rayong Refinery Co, one of the two new refiners and a joint venture of PTT and Royal Dutch Shell, is operating at about 15 percent below its 145,000-bpd capacity, a source close to the company said.
